proposedOverrides.name: Regency of Algiers
proposedOverrides.summary: The Regency of Algiers governed from the port under Ottoman affiliation. French forces took Algiers in 1830, ending the dey’s government. The city and its communities continued under colonial rule.

overrideClaims.text: The Regency of Algiers governed from the port under Ottoman affiliation. French forces took Algiers in 1830, ending the dey’s government. The city and its communities continued under colonial rule.
overrideClaims.locator: Ottoman authority and French colonization sections, 1518 and 1830.
overrideClaims.reason: Distinguish the regency represented by this historical record from a generic modern-city description.

scopeNotes: This card concerns the Regency of Algiers, with explicit continuation of city life after 1830. It is distinct from the colonial and modern Algeria card. Modern borders are not projected backward as complete Ottoman control.

Imported coverage runs from 1650 to 1878. The 1650 to 1700 polygon lies inland far southwest of the port, while later polygons cover a much larger northern territory. The early polygon’s identity and all border accuracy remain unverified. No geometry was changed.
The final imported polygon extends beyond the 1830 end of the regency. A post-regency period explains the city’s continuation, and the sourced fall year is stated separately from coverage.

The consular timeline is used for broad Ottoman affiliation and the 1830 surrender and continued resistance. Its unverified ruler counts, other ancient chronology, rhetoric and casualty totals are not adopted. The beginning around 1518 is approximate.

UNESCO’s conflicting fourth- and sixth-century ancient settlement dates and undated population estimate are omitted. Its dated assessment of building materials and urban uses is not a claim that every building is unchanged.

Lafer’s fountain counts come from different observers and years and are not compared as a consistent census. Patronal praise is treated as a public claim. The inscription and documented relocations, not the present position, establish the monument’s original context.

The Palais des Raïs history distinguishes an initial restoration launch in 1987 from actual works in 1988. The card does not infer the current condition of every building or that restoration erased its history of inhabited use.

The Walters textile is broadly attributed to Algeria, not securely to an Algiers workshop. Its unidentified maker and owner and incomplete provenance are explicit. The Met panel provides a second regional example, with no invented function or excavation context.

Treaty provisions are read as normative agreements, not proof of implementation. The 1795 text is Kramers’s 1930 translation of Turkish, whose editorial warning about the original English version is explained. It is not silently combined with the differing 1795 English version.
The 1815 agreement’s anti-enslavement and refuge clauses have specific personal and bilateral scopes. The card does not present them as universal abolition or proof that all captives were freed.
Independent historical review, border assessment and depth certification remain pending.
